title: Human Factors in Lighting
review_question: How do lighting conditions (light characteristics, sources, distribution, controls) affect human visual performance, discomfort, perception of spaces and objects, circadian rhythms, health, and behavior in various built environments (offices, industry, escape routes, driving, crime, elderly care)?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Implicitly includes research studies and practical experience related to human responses to lighting across various built environment contexts, spanning from early 20th century to 2003. No explicit formal criteria stated.

environmental_features: spectral composition (correlated color temperature, specific wavelengths)
timing of light exposure (daytime, nighttime, shift work schedules)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: Varies widely across reviewed studies, from acute (minutes/hours) to chronic (days/weeks/months)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Light exposure influences both homeostatic sleep drive (Process S) and circadian rhythm (Process C), affecting alertness and sleep timing.

Non-visual effects of light on human physiology and behavior are primarily mediated by intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) containing melanopsin, which are maximally sensitive to blue light.
The perception of discomfort glare is influenced by factors such as luminance of the glare source, background luminance, and angular size and position of the glare source.

mechanism_chain.description: Light exposure affects the human circadian system through retinal photoreceptors, leading to physiological and behavioral changes.

steps.to_construct: Activation of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)
Signal transmission to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)
Suppression of melatonin production from the pineal gland
Phase shifting of circadian rhythms and increased alertness
